rationale: Evidence: the development simulator shows 0 of 60 trials finished. Every run ended off track on all three tracks (oval, s-bend, slalom), with progress of only 0.11 to 0.15. The off-track limit is max(0.06, 0.0125 + 0.12/4) = 0.06 m, and max_error reached 0.060 to 0.068 m, so the robot drifts past the edge of the tape early in each course. RMS error (0.025 to 0.031 m) is large relative to the 0.0125 m half-width, and each run lost the line about once. Steering oscillation is modest (0.10 to 0.14), so the main problem is poor tracking, not jitter. The likely causes are that the sensors see the line only late and are too narrow to catch drift on bends, that the robot is too sluggish to correct at speed, and that a 0.12 m track with 0.8 kg mass gives a slow yaw response. Changes: (1) widen the sensor array to plus or minus 0.06 m and move it 0.05 m ahead of the axle, so the robot sees the tape edge sooner and can anticipate bends. (2) Raise kp from 3.0 to 4.5 for a stronger correction on drift, and raise kd from 0.5 to 1.0 to damp the extra gain. (3) Lower ki to 0.02 to avoid integral windup on bends. (4) Reduce base_speed from 1.6 to 1.3, so there is more time to correct at each bend; this trades some speed for control, and it is the main risk to the 3 s finish time. (5) Narrow wheel_track to 0.10 m and mass to 0.6 kg, which increases turn responsiveness. Expected result: fewer off-track exits and fewer line-loss events, with max_error below the 0.06 m limit on most seeds. Completion is possible but not certain; if speed is too low to finish in 3 s, the next iteration should raise base_speed. Measurements are kept complete so the next iteration can separate tracking error from speed effects.
